answer:
**Short answer:** It may be illegal, but the facts you have so far don't settle it. Florida law bans a landlord from raising one tenant's rent "primarily because" the tenant complained to a code enforcement agency. You complained to the city about the mold, and the increase came three days after the inspection. Your neighbors' rent stayed the same. Those facts point toward retaliation. Your landlord can still defend the increase by showing a different main reason. The law also protects you only if you complained in good faith. So the increase is not automatically unlawful, and it is not automatically fine either.

What you can do is raise retaliation if your landlord tries to evict you over the increase, for example for not paying the higher rent. I would not assume the increase is void on its own.

What was your landlord's stated reason for the increase, in the letter or in anything said to you?

DETAILS

### Does Florida law protect you from retaliation for a code complaint?
Yes. Under s. 83.64(1)(a), a landlord may not "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent" primarily because the tenant "complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises." Your April 28 complaint to city code enforcement fits that description. Your lease is a month-to-month lease in a private apartment building, so the chapter covers you.

### Does the different treatment of your neighbors matter?
Yes. Section 83.64(4) says "discrimination" means being "treated differently as to the rent charged." The statute makes that "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." You say two neighbors' rents did not change, which supports this element. This is what they told you, so it's worth confirming, ideally in writing. It also matters whether their units are similar to yours and whether they are also month-to-month. Your landlord could argue those differences explain the increase.

### Can your landlord defend the increase?
Probably, if there is a real reason other than your complaint. The statute requires that retaliation be the landlord's primary reason. Your landlord could point to market rates, a unit upgrade, or a different lease type. The timing, three days after the inspection, is strong evidence for you but does not decide the question. The statute also requires that you acted "in good faith." Nothing you've told me suggests otherwise, since the mold is not something you caused.

### How can you use this protection?
Section 83.64(2) says retaliation "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." No eviction has been filed. The statute does call retaliatory rent increases "unlawful." It does not spell out a separate way to sue over an increase before any eviction. Whether you can do that is unsettled in this text, so I can't promise it.

Under s. 83.64(3), the protection does not apply if your landlord proves an eviction is "for good cause," such as nonpayment of rent. If you stop paying or underpay, your landlord could call that good cause. I'm not advising you either way. It is a risk to know about.

### Can your landlord end the tenancy instead?
Your lease is month-to-month. Section 83.57(3) lets either side end it with "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period," and the notice must be in writing. Section 83.64(1) also bars bringing an action for possession primarily as retaliation. An eviction brought for that reason would face the same defense.

### What does your lease say about rent increases?
Clause 4 sets rent at $1,050 per month. Clause 3 makes the tenancy month-to-month. The lease has no clause on rent increases or the notice they require. Clause 10 says the lease can be changed only "in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." Whether a unilateral rent increase in a month-to-month tenancy needs your agreement is not answered by the lease or by anything I've pulled from the statute. I haven't confirmed this point.

In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith. Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where: (a) The tenant has complained to a governmental agency charged with responsibility for enforcement of a building, housing, or health code of a suspected violation applicable to the premises; (b) The tenant has organized, encouraged, or participated in a tenant organization; (c) The tenant has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1); (d) The tenant is a servicemember who has terminated a rental agreement pursuant to s. 83.682 ; (e) The tenant has paid rent to a condominium, cooperative, or homeowners’ association after demand from the association in order to pay the landlord’s obligation to the association; or (f) The tenant has exercised his or her rights under local, state, or federal fair housing laws. answer:
Probably not. Windows are normally the landlord's job. But Florida law says the landlord isn't responsible for damage caused by a guest you invited, and your lease says the same. So you probably can't force the landlord to fix this one at their own cost. The office's answer that you must pay is consistent with the law and your lease. Holding back rent or ending the lease over this window would likely fail, because both depend on the landlord's repair duty.

Has the office given you an amount or a deadline for the repair?

DETAILS

### Is a window the landlord's job?
Usually, yes. Under § 83.51(1)(b), where no building, housing or health codes apply, the landlord must maintain "windows, doors, floors" and other structural parts "in good repair." Whether a local code covers your window is outside what I can check. The city or county code office can tell you. Your home is a unit in a larger building, so the statute gives no way to change this duty by a written agreement. Your lease has no repair clause that shifts window repair to you in general.

### Does it matter that your friend broke it?
Yes. Section 83.51(4) says "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." You told me your invited friend was roughhousing and fell into the window. That means a guest you let in caused it. The breakage being an accident doesn't clearly change that, because the law covers negligent acts, not only deliberate ones. How a court would see "roughhousing" is a judgment call that I can't settle.

### What does your lease say?
Section 11 says: "Tenant shall pay for repairing damage caused by Tenant, Tenant's household, or Tenant's guests." It also says to report repairs "in writing through the resident portal." You did that on February 2. Section 11's list of things the landlord keeps in working order names the refrigerator, stove, dishwasher and central air conditioning. It doesn't name windows.

### Can you end the lease or hold back rent?
- **Ending the lease (§ 83.56(1)):** This requires the landlord to fail a repair duty under § 83.51(1) or a material lease promise. Section 83.51(4) takes this window out of that duty, and your lease puts guest damage on you.
- **Holding back rent (§ 83.60(1)(b)):** This works only for a failure of the § 83.51(1) duty. It carries the risk of an eviction case. The same § 83.51(4) problem applies.
- **Your February rent:** You paid it on February 1, before the party. So you haven't paid rent knowing about this problem.

### What about the cold?
I can't make the landlord pay for this repair. Heat is a separate duty under § 83.51(2)(a)5 ("Functioning facilities for heat during winter"). That duty is about the heating system, not a broken window, and § 83.51(4) still applies to damage from your guest. A faster route may be to arrange the repair yourself, or to ask the office to do it and bill you under § 11. I can't say what that would cost you, or whether the landlord could later take it from your deposit. That is outside what I can check here.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently from other tenants, in rent, services, or action taken, is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.

answer:
**Short answer:** It's not settled whether you can move out now and stop paying rent. Your notice and the 7-day wait look fine. The open points are whether a hot water failure counts under the section that lets you end the lease, and whether paying March rent gave up that right. If you leave and a court later reads those points against you, you could owe rent for the rest of the lease. You haven't told the landlord you'll withhold rent, so you can't simply stay and stop paying either. Have you contacted the city or county code office about the hot water?

DETAILS

### Did your letter work as the required notice?
It looks like it did.
- Under 83.56(1), the notice must be written. It must name the problem and say you intend to end the lease because of it.
- Your letter says the water heater is broken and that you'll end the lease if it isn't fixed within 7 days. That matches.
- Section 83.56(4) says notices go "by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof," or by e-mail under 83.505. Certified mail is mailing.
- Lease §7 also allows certified mail to the office, and the statute says notice rules can't be waived in the lease (83.56(4)).
- A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord. The office signed for yours on March 9, so the 7 days ran to March 16. That date has passed, and the heater is still not fixed.

### Is hot water a duty that lets you end the lease?
This is not settled. Section 83.56(1) reaches only the landlord's duties under 83.51(1) and "material provisions of the rental agreement."
- Your lease says nothing about hot water or repairs, so no lease promise helps you here.
- **Reading one:** A water heater is part of the plumbing. Section 83.51(1)(b) requires "the plumbing in reasonable working condition." Under this reading it's an 83.51(1) duty, and ending the lease is available.
- **Reading two:** Section 83.51(2)(a)5 names "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water" as a separate duty for apartment buildings like yours. Under this reading it's a subsection (2) duty, which 83.56(1) doesn't mention.
- Section 83.51(3) says that if the subsection (1) duty is the same or greater, subsection (1) controls. Whether it is the same or greater here is the open question.
- A local building, housing, or health code might also cover hot water (83.51(1)(a)). The codes aren't stored in this tool, so the code office would have to tell you.

### Is the failure "material"?
This is not settled, because the statute doesn't define the word.
- **One reading:** Any failure of a listed duty is material.
- **Other reading:** It depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
- No hot water since February 25 and no reply to your letter would support you under either reading.

### Did paying March rent give up your right?
This is not settled. You paid on March 1, after the problem began on February 25. Section 83.56(5)(a) says a tenant who "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" waives the right to end the lease "for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance."
- **Reading one:** An unfixed heater is a continuing noncompliance, so paying rent gave up nothing.
- **Reading two:** Paying with knowledge gave up the right to end the lease over this failure, and only a new failure would start over.

### Can you just stop paying rent and stay?
No, not on what you've sent so far.
- Holding back rent as a defense needs a separate written notice saying you won't pay rent because of the problem. You then wait 7 days after it's delivered (83.60(1)(b)). Your letter only says you'll end the lease.
- That defense covers only 83.51(1) duties. Section 83.51(2)(c) says a subsection (2) failure can't be raised as a defense to an eviction for nonpayment. So the same hot water question applies here too.
- Holding back rent risks an eviction case. If you're sued, you must pay the rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within the time the summons gives. If you don't, you lose your defenses (83.60(2)).

### What else can you do?
- **Damages:** Section 83.55 lets you recover damages caused by the landlord's failure. Rent paid with knowledge may also affect your right to sue, as in the waiver question above (83.56(5)(a)).
- **Code complaint:** A complaint to the code office can lead to an inspection. Section 83.64(1) protects you from retaliation for a good-faith complaint or a repair notice.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently from other tenants, in rent, services, or action taken, is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.

answer:
**Short answer:** I wouldn't hold back rent over these two items. Florida's rent-withholding protection covers only the basic repair duties in the statute. Your lease promises the dishwasher, and the pool is a lease amenity. Neither is one of those statutory duties. If you stop paying and your landlord files for eviction, the law likely wouldn't protect you. You also haven't sent the kind of written notice that withholding needs. Your two portal requests asked for repairs but didn't say you would stop paying rent. You do have other options, including damages and, in some cases, ending the lease.

DETAILS

### Can you hold back rent over a dishwasher and a pool?
- The withholding defense covers only "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" (83.60(1)(b)). Section 83.51(1) covers building, housing and health codes, and structural parts and plumbing. A dishwasher and a pool are not on that list.
- Whether a local code covers either one is outside what I can check. Your city or county code office could tell you.
- The dishwasher is a lease promise. Lease section 11 says your landlord "will keep them in working order," and the dishwasher is listed there. That makes it a lease duty, not an 83.51(1) duty.
- Withholding is risky. The landlord could file an eviction case for nonpayment. If that happens, you must pay the rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within the deadline in the summons (83.60(2)). If you miss it, you lose your defenses other than payment.

### What about the pool?
- Lease section 11 says residents "may use the community pool from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.". It also says "Landlord may close the pool for cleaning, repairs, or weather." A pump repair fits that wording.
- It is not settled whether this clause limits the pool promise, so I'm not picking a side.
  - **Reading one:** the clause only describes what the lease promises. A closure for repairs is then allowed, and the pool gives you little claim.
  - **Reading two:** a clause that cuts off your rights under this law is void to that extent (83.47(1)(a)). A closure with no end date could then still be a failure to provide the pool.
- Whether a clause that limits an amenity counts as such a clause is not settled.

### Can you end the lease over the dishwasher?
Maybe, but you haven't taken the first step. Section 83.56(1) lets you end the lease if your landlord "materially fails" to meet a lease provision within 7 days after your written notice. That notice must say what is wrong and that you intend to end the lease.
- **Your notice:** your portal requests don't qualify. A portal message isn't a delivery method the statute names (83.56(4)). Lease section 7 requires hand delivery to Suite A or certified mail. Your portal requests also didn't mention ending the lease.
- **"Material":** the statute doesn't define it, so it is unsettled. One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts. The other looks at how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
- **Rent you paid:** you paid May rent on 2026-05-01, after you knew about the problem. Under 83.56(5)(a), paying rent with knowledge waives the right to end the lease "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." Whether an unfixed dishwasher counts as continuing is unsettled. One reading says paying gave up nothing because the problem continues. The other says the payment gave up that right for this failure.

### What else can you do?
- **Damages:** you can seek the damages caused by a failure to meet the lease (83.55). Paying rent with knowledge may affect the right to sue (83.56(5)(a)), with the same two readings as above. The winner in a suit may recover attorney fees and costs (83.48). Amounts are outside this tool.
- **Code complaint:** you can ask the code office whether either problem violates a local code. The law protects tenants from retaliation for a good-faith code complaint or a proper notice (83.64(1)).
- **Landlord can't fix it:** if the pool pump problem is beyond your landlord's control and your landlord is making every reasonable effort, 83.56(1)(b) says rent for the period of noncompliance "shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value." Whether that applies depends on what your landlord has done. It is also unsettled whether the parties must agree to the change.

Has your landlord told you anything, in any form, about when the pool pump or the dishwasher will be fixed?

Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Never give a date for those 5 days; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently from other tenants, in rent, services, or action taken, is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.

answer:
**Short answer:** Not yet. If you skip May rent now, your landlord could file for eviction, and you would have no protected defense. Florida lets you hold back rent over a roof leak only after you give a written notice. The notice must say you won't pay rent because of the problem, and 7 days must pass after it reaches your landlord. Your two phone calls don't count, because the law requires the notice to be in writing. Whether this leak is serious enough to count as a "material" failure is not settled. Even if you do everything right, holding back rent is a risk, and a court decides whether the defense works.

DETAILS

### Does Florida's landlord-tenant law cover your home?
Almost certainly yes. Your lease is with a property management company for an apartment, and nothing in it ties your housing to a school. None of the exclusions in 83.42 appear to fit. I've saved "no school housing" as a pending fact for you to confirm.

### Is the roof your landlord's job?
Yes. Your landlord must "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair" (83.51(1)(b)). A local building code may also apply. The code office can tell you, and I can't check that. The landlord isn't responsible for damage the tenant causes (83.51(4)). You told me rain caused this and you did nothing to cause it. Your lease has no repair clause that changes this, and for an apartment building the statute doesn't allow the landlord's roof duty to be changed in writing.

### What does the law require before you can hold back rent?
Section 83.60(1)(b) allows the defense only "if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof."
- **What the notice says:** It names the leak and says you will not pay rent because of it. A letter that only asks for a repair is not enough.
- **When the 7 days start:** They start on the day the notice reaches your landlord, not the day you send it. I can't count the days until I know that delivery date.
- **How to deliver it:** The statute doesn't say how, and that is unsettled. One reading is that any written notice that reaches the manager or the person who collects rent counts, including a portal message or e-mail. The other reading is that part II's delivery methods apply (83.56(4)), so a portal message or text wouldn't count. Your lease says no e-mail delivery was agreed (§8). Handing it to the office or mailing it satisfies both readings. Lease §7 says to hand it to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail.

### What happens if your landlord sues?
If your landlord files for eviction, you must pay the rent the complaint claims into the court registry. You must also keep paying rent into the registry as it comes due while the case runs (83.60(2)). Alternatively, you must file a motion to set that amount within 5 days (not counting weekends and holidays) after you are served. Missing that deadline waives your defenses except proof of payment (83.60(2)). The summons will state this requirement. If a court agrees the failure is material, the leak is a complete defense to eviction for nonpayment. The court then decides how much, if any, your rent is reduced (83.60(1)(b)).

### Other paths: ending the lease, damages, and a code complaint
- **Ending the lease:** A written notice that says you will end the lease, followed by 7 days without a repair, may let you do that (83.56(1)). You paid April rent after you knew about the leak. Under 83.56(5)(a), paying rent with knowledge gives up the right to end the lease or sue over that failure, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." Whether a leak that is still unfixed counts as continuing is not settled. One reading is that it does, so paying gave up nothing. The other is that paying gave up the right over this failure.
- **Damages:** You may be able to recover damages caused by the landlord's failure (83.55). The same 83.56(5)(a) question applies.
- **Code complaint:** A complaint to the city or county code office is another route. Retaliation, such as a rent increase or an eviction filing aimed at you for complaining in good faith, is unlawful (83.64). A landlord can still act for good cause, such as nonpayment of rent.

Which of these is best for you depends on whether you want to stay or leave.

Has the manager said anything on your calls about when, or whether, the roof will be fixed?
